text: Rain gathers on the last leaf of the branch. The leaf bends, lets one drop go, and rises a little. Below it, a fern is dark with water.
At the edge of the pond, the reeds keep their narrow spaces. A beetle crosses the water between them. Its small wake opens, widens, and is gone before it reaches the bank.
Snow has filled the hollow in the old gatepost. In the field beyond, each tuft of grass has its own white roof. The path ends at the gate. The snow goes on.
The tide has left a shallow pool in the rock. Inside it, a strand of green weed moves back and forth. The sea is farther away now, but the pool has kept this small part of its motion.
Late light rests on the garden wall. One pear hangs above it, yellow on the side toward the sun. A leaf turns and lays its shadow on the pear, then turns away.

Along the river, the willow tips touch their own reflections. The water carries each reflection a little downstream and makes another. From the bank comes the soft, dry sound of a bird moving through leaves.
The rain stopped an hour ago. Under the hedge it is still arriving, drop by drop, on last year's leaves. A blackbird turns one over. Beneath it, the earth is the color of tea.
There is a bend in the stream where the foam stays for a while. A few white flecks turn in the shade of an alder, keeping no particular distance. One slips out into the current. The others turn.
Evening moves up the hillside. First the path is cool, then the lower branches. At the top of the tallest tree, a few leaves still hold the sun.
Beyond the open window, bamboo brushes bamboo. The sound is slight enough that the spaces between it belong to the room. On the sill, a moth has folded its wings.
The cup has left a pale circle on the table. Beside it lies a teaspoon, a little warm at one end. The kitchen window is open, and the curtain lifts just clear of the sill.
The cat is asleep on a folded towel. One paw has slipped over the edge. When the sun moves off the towel, the paw stays where it is.
A loaf cools on the wooden board. Once in a while its crust gives a small crack. Flour lies in the grain of the wood, and the room smells faintly of the oven.
The dishes are drying in the rack. A bead of water grows beneath the blue bowl, holds for a moment, then falls. Through the open door comes the smell of the lilac by the steps.
A patch of sunlight reaches the foot of the bed. It warms the quilt's faded squares, then the plain white sheet. The book beside the pillow is open where it fell.
The sweater has been mended with a slightly darker blue. From across the room the repair disappears. Up close, the new wool makes a small soft island at the elbow.
Someone has put fresh water in the jug. The mint stems lean against the glass, their lower leaves bright through the water. On the table, a single fallen leaf rests beside the handle.
The radiator clicks once. On the chair beside it, a pair of wool socks is drying. The room is dim except for the lamp and the narrow light under the kitchen door.
The last page of the newspaper is folded under the seed trays. Little squares of damp earth sit in rows. In one of them, a green loop has risen since breakfast.
A spoon of honey settles in the warm milk. For a while a gold thread hangs below the surface. Then the thread grows pale, and the milk is still.

Rain on the shed roof.
Under the eaves,
a dry place
just wide enough for a sparrow.

The pond keeps
a little of the sky
between the leaves.

One warm stone
on the evening step.
The sun has gone
as far as the garden wall.

A feather rests
on the unused oar.
Water touches the boat
and lets it go.

The kettle is quiet.
In the cup,
the last small circle
widens.

At the bottom of the garden,
the gate stands open
onto more grass.

A white bowl.
Three plums.
The afternoon
on their skins.

The branch lifts
after the bird.
A leaf keeps moving
a little longer.

Folded linen
in a wicker basket.
The smell of the line
still in it.

The stream passes
under the footbridge.
On the rail,
a snail.

She carried the chair into the garden and found one leg sank into the grass. She moved it a little. Now it stood level beneath the apple tree. By the time she sat down, a petal had landed on the seat.
He opened the book where the ribbon lay. A pressed leaf slipped into his lap. He held it by its stem, then placed it on the windowsill. Outside, the tree it came from was green again.
The baker swept the last flour from the counter. At the back door, she shook the cloth over the grass. A sparrow came down to look. She left the door open while she washed her hands.
At the landing, he loosened the rope just enough for the boat to move with the water. It drifted a hand's width from the post and back. He sat on the step above it, where the wood was dry.
She took the washing off the line while it was still warm. A ladybird rode in on a pillowcase. At the kitchen window she held up a finger, and it walked onto the sill.
The child set a leaf in the stream and followed it to the bend. There it caught beside a stone. After a while the water turned it gently, and it went on. The child stayed to watch the water.
He had brought two cups to the porch. His neighbor came through the gap in the hedge and took the one nearest the steps. They watched a small bird work along the fence, stopping at every post.
She pulled the blanket over the sleeping dog's feet. One foot came out again. She left it there and sat beside the window, where the rain made the streetlights soft.
At the end of the afternoon, he put the brushes in a jar of clean water. A little blue loosened from the bristles. It spread through the jar until there was no edge to it.
She went out to close the greenhouse and found the air inside still warm. The tomato leaves had their evening smell. She watered the small pots by the door, then stood a moment among them.

The porch looks onto a small stretch of grass and the pale trunks of three birches. Rain has darkened the boards beyond the roof. Near the chair, where the wood is dry, a curled leaf moves whenever the air comes through. From somewhere in the wet garden, water drops into water.

In the reading room, the lamps have been lit although the windows are still blue. A page turns at the far end of the table. The carpet softens the sound of someone coming in. On the desk by the door, a glass of water holds a square of evening light.

The small harbor is sheltered from the wind. Reflections of the houses stretch down between the boats, red and cream and the gray of the sky. A loose rope taps the side of a hull. The water lifts it clear, then lowers it to the wood again.

The bathhouse is empty in the late afternoon. Light through a high window falls across the pale tiles. A wooden ladle floats beside its bucket, its handle resting on the rim. The water that spilled onto the floor has gathered in the shallow grooves between the tiles.

In the orchard, the grass is long enough to hide the fallen apples. Their scent rises when the air moves. Under one tree the branches make a patch of deep shade, cool even now, and the rough trunk holds a narrow stripe of sun.

The room above the bakery is warm at the floor. There is a plain chair, a table, and a window left slightly open. On the sill, a pot of thyme has grown toward the light. Downstairs, someone slides a tray onto a shelf. The sound reaches the room softly, through the boards.

At low tide the sand has fine ridges, each with a line of water in it. Clouds pass through those narrow lines. Farther out, a gull stands in the shallows, and its reflection reaches almost to its feet.

The greenhouse glass is clouded at the corners. Inside, the leaves overlap in every shade of green. Water stands in the lip of a clay saucer. From the pot above it, a drop falls slowly enough for the surface to become smooth between drops.

The courtyard has one tree and a stone basin. A little water runs into the basin from a copper pipe, making a hollow note. The shade of the tree reaches the wall behind it. In the shade, the stone keeps the cool of the morning.

Dusk settles in the room by degrees. The white curtain stays light after the wall has dimmed. The rim of the glass is visible a little longer than the table beneath it. Outside, the last bird calls once from the hedge. The window is still open.
On the windowsill: a stone from the beach, a spool of green thread, a jar with nothing in it but the afternoon light.
The little map ends at the garden gate. Beyond the gate, the path curves out of sight. On the paper, someone has drawn the apple tree with more care than anything else.

A note on the kitchen table:

The plums are ripe.
There are more in the bowl by the window.
I left the blue cup out for you.
The cupboard door has a patch where the varnish has worn away. A thumb fits there. When the door is shut, the patch is the color of the breadboard beside it.
A small history of the stone on the desk: water rounded it; a hand carried it; the window light moves across it every afternoon.

Morning, in the bowl: a pear and its shadow.
Afternoon: the same pear, a shorter shadow.
Evening: the pear, pale beside the open window.
The space between two stitches is smaller than a seed. The needle comes through, the thread follows, and the cloth gathers softly in the hand.
A loose page in a gardening book lists what grew that year. Beans. Mint. Three sunflowers. Beneath them, in a different ink: the mint came back.
There is a bench with a smooth place at each end. Rain collects in the middle. By afternoon, the dry places have joined, and a leaf has settled where the water was.

At the loom, she slips a wooden ruler beneath the finished cloth and lifts it toward her. The weave opens around the wood. There is a gray thread she nearly took out this morning; now it runs through the cream like the faint crease in a folded letter. She leaves it. When she loosens the cloth from the frame, it gathers in her lap, heavier and softer than it looked while stretched. Her hands rest beneath it for a moment before she folds it.

The quilt lies across two chairs while its maker works on the binding. Around each corner she eases the strip of fabric into place with her thumbnail. A square near the middle still has a pocket in it, from the shirt it used to be. She has sewn the pocket shut, but its rounded bottom remains, and the pale mark of a missing button. The quilt slips a little as she turns it. She draws it back over her knees and smooths the corner flat.

He winds the last of the wool around his fingers, then around the little bundle they have made. The ball grows unevenly, with a soft bulge on one side. Across the table his sister is undoing a scarf that came out too narrow. The loose wool keeps the shape of its stitches for a while, a row of little bends, before it reaches his hands. Between them the unfinished scarf grows shorter. The ball sits warm in his palm.

The ironing board stands in the spare room, beside a basket of pillowcases. She presses one seam, lifts the iron, and turns the cloth. A faint scent of warm cotton rises. Through the doorway she can hear someone finding a tune on a piano, slowly, one hand at a time. She folds the pillowcase around the seam she has just pressed. The corners meet. In the basket below, the next one has a small embroidered branch, nearly the same white as the cloth.

In the sewing drawer, the ribbons have worked themselves loose from their cards. She rolls the broad brown one around two fingers. It has a satin side and a dull side, and each turn shows a little of both. The green ribbon is only long enough to tie around a small parcel. She winds that too. At the bottom of the drawer she finds a button still threaded with red, and puts it in the shallow tin with the others.

The potter stops the wheel with the side of her foot. For several turns the wet clay continues to shine, then the same pale mark stays facing her. She draws a wire beneath the pot and lifts its board to the shelf. Inside, the walls bear the small ridges her fingers left. They will be there after the clay has dried. She washes her hands in the basin, rubbing each finger clean, and rests the board on its wooden supports.

A row of clay dishes dries beneath a sheet of cloth. At the end of the row, one has a shallow thumbprint near the rim. The potter had picked it up before it was ready. She lifts the cloth to look, touches the dry edge with the back of a finger, and lays the cloth down again. Its weight makes a little tent above each dish. A corner hangs over the shelf, moving slightly in the air from the open door.

He pours the slip from one jug to another. It falls in a broad, quiet ribbon and closes over the bottom without a splash. On the workbench, yesterday's clay has dried pale around the handles of the tools. He loosens it with a wet sponge. The bench darkens beneath his hand. When he has finished, a clean rectangle of wood shows where a damp cloth lay all morning, and the jugs stand beside it, full to different heights.

The kiln has been cold since morning. She opens its door and stands beside it before reaching in. A little dish sits on the upper shelf, its glaze the color of oat husks. At the bottom of the dish the glaze has gathered darker, in the shallow place where water will collect. She turns it once between her hands. Then she sets it on a folded cloth and takes out the next piece.

The child makes a small clay house without a roof. Inside he presses a seat against one wall and a round table against another. His grandmother holds the base steady while he fits the door. Their fingers have left overlapping marks around the outside. He asks where the people will sleep. She points to the soft piece of clay left on the board, and together they roll out a bed.

The pantry is cooler than the kitchen. A stone shelf runs along the back wall, with jars of lentils and a paper sack folded over at the top. She sets the butter dish in its usual hollow and slides a plate of cut melon beside it. The door stays open while she searches for a clean cloth. From the kitchen comes the sound of a drawer closing. Here, on the stone, the melon is already cooling at the edges.

In the cellar, the potatoes lie under a length of sacking. Beside them, onions hang in loose braids from a nail. He comes down for one and stays to straighten the paper beneath the basket. The stairs make a dark triangle on the whitewashed wall. When he goes up, he carries the onion loosely, its dry skin turning against his wrist. He leaves the cellar door ajar for the cool air.

She opens the biscuit tin and finds the folded paper her father always puts beneath the lid. He has written the baking date on it, small and neat, beside a butter mark. The biscuits are arranged on their sides, close enough to hold one another up. She takes two and eases the others together. The lid settles into its groove with a low metal sound. On the worktop, a crumb has stayed where the tin was.

The kitchen floor has been washed. At its far edge, the damp strip beneath the cupboard is still a little darker. The chairs stand upside down on the table, their worn feet showing four small felt circles apiece. She opens the back door and sits on the threshold to wait for the boards to dry. The air near the floor is cool. By the time she gets up, the last dark strip has narrowed to a line.

A blue cloth covers the dough in the pantry. The cloth has risen just enough to lift one corner clear of the dish. He comes in to fetch the salt and brushes the flour from its lid with his thumb. On the shelf below, the folded kitchen towels smell of the wooden drawer where they were kept. He takes one, closes the salt, and leaves the dough beneath its small, rounded hill of cloth.

Her brother arrives with a bag of groceries and begins putting things away. He places the heavy jars on the lower shelf, where she can reach them without lifting her arm. Neither mentions it. They talk about the new paint on the corner shop while he folds the paper bag along its old creases. Before he goes, he moves the stool back beneath the counter. She finds the biscuits later, beside her favorite plate.

The child has fallen asleep with one sock on. His father sits on the edge of the mattress and eases the other over his heel. At the toes, the sock has a loose fold. He smooths it with two fingers. Downstairs someone is rinsing the supper plates, setting each one into the rack with a small space between. He stays until the child's hand opens on the cover, then lowers the lamp.

At the end of lunch, her aunt peels an orange in one long strip. She breaks the fruit into sections and places the smallest beside the child's hand. He is watching the peel curl back on itself. For a while they leave it between them. Then he lifts one end and rolls it inward, slowly, until it makes a little orange rose on the empty plate.

He has brought back her scarf. She had left it on the peg after their walk, and he folded it around a sprig of rosemary from beside his door. The scarf is cool from outside. She hangs it over the back of a chair and puts the rosemary in a dish. Later, when she passes, she stops to turn the folded end inward so it will not trail on the floor. A few needles have fallen on the seat.

The two sisters shell peas into a wide pan. One opens the pods and passes them over; the other runs her thumb along each seam. When they reach a very small pea, they set it beside the pan, where a few others are already gathered. Their mother used to call those the ones for the spoon. After a while one sister brings a spoon from the drawer and lays it beside the little green heap.

The carpenter hangs his apron on the nail behind the door. A curl of pale wood stays caught in its pocket. On the bench, a new drawer stands open to show the smooth base and the pencil mark he has not rubbed away. He slides it in slowly. Near the end it settles into place under its own weight. He opens it once more and closes it with his fingertips.

In the bookbinder's room, the glue is cooling in its jar. A repaired volume rests between two clean boards, held by a weight wrapped in cloth. She gathers the little offcuts from the table. Some are narrow enough to curl around the blade of her scissors. Under the press lies a strip of dark green cloth, the same cloth now covering the book's spine. She folds it and keeps it in the drawer.

He cleans the violin with a soft piece of flannel. Around the bridge he works more slowly, lifting the powder from beneath each string. The instrument rests on his knees, its back shaped to the hollow there. When he puts it in its case, he tucks the flannel beside the neck. The lid stays open while he returns the chair to the table.

The last basket stands beside the workbench with a damp towel over its rim. Its maker has tucked in the ends of the willow and trimmed the place where the handle joins. On the floor, the discarded lengths curve around her shoes. She gathers them into a loose ring. The basket will dry by morning; for now its sides are dark, and the handle feels cool against her palm.

The clockmaker has finished for the day. She lays the tiny screws in a lidded dish and draws the cloth over the open case. On a shelf behind her, the repaired clock makes its ordinary sound. She had listened closely all afternoon. Now she hears it from across the room while she washes the basin, each little stroke reaching her through the open workshop door.

Frost has grown from the lower corners of the window. Near the latch, it spreads into a fern with several uneven fronds. The room beyond the glass is warming. A clear bead forms at the tip of the longest frond, gathers more water, and slides into the narrow wooden channel below. The pattern remains around the place it left, a little thinner now.

The clothesline is white with frost. From the kitchen window it looks thicker than it did yesterday, though every strand is still visible near the post. Along the fence, a spider's empty web holds a row of pale beads. The gate has been left on its latch. In the small gap beneath it, the grass is dark and soft.

He brings a log in from the shed. The bark is cold beneath his fingers, and a dry scrap loosens onto the mat. He lays the log beside the hearth with the others. For a few minutes the frost in its creases stays white. Then the bark darkens in narrow lines, and the scrap on the mat uncurls.

On the frozen pond, a thin reed leans across its own pale outline. Beneath the ice there are strings of bubbles, each ending where the water held it. A child has left one mitten on the rail. Someone has turned it thumb-up and tucked the cuff around the wood, so it will stay there until they return.

The wool curtain has drawn back a little from the window. Through the opening, the frost is white against the early sky. On the room side, the cloth has a deep crease where it has hung folded all night. She runs a hand down it, then lets it fall. Its hem brushes the floor and stays there.

In the waiting room, a woman is sewing a button onto her coat. The coat rests across her lap, and the thread makes a small loop after each pass of the needle. Across from her, someone who has been sitting very straight settles back into the chair. She winds the thread around the stem of the button and knots it underneath. The room has a little more space between its sounds.

He lies on the rug with a folded towel beneath his head. Above him, the ceiling has the faint outline of a repair he made years ago. He follows its uneven edge to where the white paint becomes smooth again. Somewhere along the passage a slipper brushes the floor. The towel warms beneath his cheek; his fingers loosen against the weave of the rug.

The train has stopped at a small station. Through the open carriage door comes the smell of cut grass. A porter stands beside an empty trolley, one hand over the other on its handle. Inside, the fabric of a passenger's sleeve rises slightly, falls, and rests against the seat. The trolley wheel turns a fraction under the porter's hand. Along the platform, the grass cuttings lie in a thin, even row.

She sits on the floor while her daughter braids her hair. Now and then a small hand rests on her shoulder to keep the braid straight. The child works carefully near the ends, where the hair keeps slipping loose. She finds a ribbon in her pocket, ties a bow, and spreads it flat. Her mother stays where she is, the braid warm against the back of her neck.

His head has settled against the back of the chair. The book lies open on his knees, one finger still between the pages. In the kitchen, the refrigerator stops humming. For a little while the room seems larger. He moves his hand from the book to the arm of the chair, where the fabric has worn smooth, and the pages slowly close.

The drawer used to catch halfway in. She has rubbed a little wax along its runner and brushed away the loose dust. Now it slides without the lift she always gave it. She tries it twice, then puts the tea towels back, folded edge outward. When she closes it, the handle comes to rest exactly where her hand expects it.

He replaces the felt beneath the chair leg. The old piece peels away in a small gray circle; the new one is thick enough to press with a thumb. He sets the chair upright and eases it toward the table. It moves almost soundlessly across the boards. Under the table, his shoes find the familiar crossbar.

The little wooden box opens flat again. Its owner has tightened the hinge and rubbed the lid with a clean cloth. Inside are several lengths of string, a brass key, and a photograph face down. She puts the key into the shallow groove worn by years of being kept there. Then she closes the lid. The two sides meet without the gap.

He has sewn the lining back into her coat. Around the pocket, he used small uneven stitches because the cloth was thin. She slips her hand in and finds the seam smooth beneath her fingers. From the other pocket she takes a folded shopping list, too old to need now. She smooths it on the table while he puts away the needle.

The loose tile beside the step has been set back in place. Around its edge, the new mortar is a darker gray. By evening it will be pale like the rest. A mason has left a little piece of board across it, and moved the flowerpot just far enough aside for someone to pass. Behind the pot, the old patch of wall is still dry.

At her father's house, she still knows which drawer holds the good scissors. She opens it and finds them beneath a folded cloth, with the same length of string tied through one handle. He is in the next room turning the radio dial. A few clear notes arrive, and he leaves it there. She cuts the ribbon around the parcel and folds it into the drawer beside the scissors.

The schoolroom has been turned into a village sewing room. Along the wall, the old coat pegs remain at a child's height. She hangs her bag on the one nearest the door and sits beneath the map. Someone has repaired a corner of it with tape. The sea is the blue she remembers. While the others measure their fabric, she traces the edge of her scissors against the table's shallow initials.

He finds the blanket from the long car journeys at the bottom of the cupboard. Its checked edge has gone soft, and a little road grit still lies in the fold. He carries it outside and shakes it over the bare paving. The cloth opens wide, then hangs from his hands. When he brings it in, he lays it over the armchair with the smooth, faded side uppermost.

The holiday house still has its old bread bin. She lifts the curved lid and smells the dry wood inside. Her grandmother used to keep a clean knife beneath the loaf, its handle wrapped in a corner of the cloth. She puts the bread she has brought in the same place. The lid rolls down, and her hand follows its curve to the counter.

They have kept the low mark on the kitchen doorframe. He stands beside it now, much taller, while his mother searches for the pencil she always used. She finds it in a drawer, short enough to rest in her palm. Beneath his new mark, the earlier lines crowd together in the wood. She brushes the shavings from the shelf with the side of her hand.

They sit at opposite ends of the worktable, each with a piece of paper. He is drawing the room; she is writing a letter. Now and then one of them moves the lamp a little, and the other moves closer to its light. After a while he turns his drawing around. She rests her pen across the page and looks. In his picture, her slippers touch the rung of his chair.

The small room has been swept. In the corner, a broom rests with its bristles turned away from the wall. There are two cushions on the floor, one with a deeper hollow in it. The door opens inward and stops just short of the woven mat. From another room comes the sound of someone laying a table, then the soft tread of feet along the passage.

She is sorting the photographs while he makes room in the album. Sometimes she hands him one and waits for him to turn it over. On the back, in his mother's writing, there is usually a place and a month. They leave the oldest pictures on the table, where the corners have begun to curl. Beside them, the album lies open to a clean page.

The visitor sits beside the open sewing box. Her friend has gone to find the right shade of thread. In the lid, a ribbon holds a small pair of scissors; below it, the needles lie threaded through a scrap of felt. She rests her hand on the edge of the table. The floor creaks down the hall, and her friend returns holding two spools against her sleeve.

At the community kitchen, the last two people fold the tablecloth. Each holds a corner and walks toward the other until the edges meet. They lay it on the table, press out the crease, and fold it once more. The room smells of clean plates and warm wood. One opens the cupboard; the other puts the cloth on the shelf.

The shuttle rests
halfway through the loom.
Beneath it,
the cloth hangs loose.

Her hand is still
beneath the child's head.
The storybook
has slipped shut.

The repaired drawer opens.
Inside, a folded cloth
keeps the shape
of the shelf above.

Frost at the window's edge.
In the clear middle,
the room's small lamp.

The clay is dry.
A thumbprint remains
where the handle
meets the pot.

The tailor keeps the short lengths of thread in a shallow dish. At the end of the day she draws them out one by one, laying the useful ones across her palm. A red length catches around her finger. She loosens it, winds it onto a card, and slips the end beneath the last turn. There is a low stool under the table for a child to sit on during a fitting. She straightens it with her foot. Then she covers the sewing machine, letting the cloth settle over the wheel, the spool, the little shelf where her scissors lie.

The lamp in the hallway has a cloth shade. Its lower edge is coming loose, and he sits beneath it with a needle while she holds the ladder steady. He takes a small stitch, moves the shade a little, and takes another. The cloth makes a pale circle above them. When the seam is finished, he turns the lamp on. The join shows as a fine line in the weave. They stand for a moment looking up, then fold the ladder and carry it back through the kitchen, one at each end.

The room at the back of the museum holds only a loom, a wooden bench, and several lengths of finished cloth. A keeper comes in to close the shutters. She leaves the last one halfway open while a visitor ties his shoe. From the bench he can see the cloth on the loom, its lower edge rolled around a smooth beam. The loose fringe hangs above the floor. He finishes the knot and sits a moment longer. The keeper leans against the doorframe, keys gathered into her hand.

She brings a chair into the room where her father is taking apart an old radio. He has spread the screws on a white handkerchief, each one beside the place it will return to. She tells him about the new footpath behind the houses. He listens while he turns a little wheel with one finger. A clear voice comes through, followed by the opening notes of a song. He replaces the back of the radio, leaves the screws on the cloth, and turns his chair toward hers.

The bathwater has cooled enough for her to trail a hand in it. On the stool beside the tub, a towel has been folded with the worn patch hidden underneath. Through the wall she hears a cupboard being closed and the light footsteps of someone going upstairs. She lifts her hand. Water follows the curve of her wrist, gathers at her elbow, and falls. The surface moves toward the sides of the tub and back, each return a little lower, until the pale ceiling lies in it again.
